title: Maitreya's tower
hookLine: Sudhana enters a tower where every room holds all the others

cards: The door is shut. Sudhana stands outside a great tower, at the end of city after city and teacher after teacher, and he can't get in. So he waits.

He walks around it with respect, and he hopes. Then the owner comes up the road with a crowd around him. It's Maitreya, the bodhisattva who, Buddhists say, will be the next Buddha, the same Maitreya from Asanga's story.
Sudhana asks to be let in, and what happens next turns the whole road inside out.

teach.b: Maitreya doesn't use a key. He snaps his fingers, and the door opens. Sudhana steps in, the door closes behind him, and the inside is bigger than the outside.

The tower is as wide as the sky, and within it are other towers, more than he can count, each one as vast and as beautifully made. Here's the part to slow down for. Those towers don't crowd each other.
Each one is whole, and each sits inside the others without pushing anything out of the way. Every room holds all the rooms, and every room is still its own.
In them Sudhana sees scenes from Maitreya's long path: Maitreya first setting out, practicing, teaching, giving. He even sees himself there, standing in front of each scene.
A few days ago, Indra's net was a picture to think about. Here, the young pilgrim walks around inside it. Then Maitreya snaps his fingers again, and the vision is over.
Sudhana is standing in an ordinary tower. Where did it all go, he asks. Maitreya's answer is gentle.

It didn't come from anywhere, and it hasn't gone anywhere. It arose from conditions, the way a dream does, or a magic show, and it rests the same way. In the sutra's telling, it isn't a trick to fool Sudhana.
It's how everything works, shown all at once.
A kitchen can hold every meal ever cooked in it, a song can hold a whole summer, and neither gets any larger.

how: Readers of the Flower Garland Sutra in East Asian Buddhism treat Sudhana's vision in Maitreya's tower as a high point of his pilgrimage and a picture of how all things contain one another.

games.q: you're Sudhana, outside the closed tower. Maitreya arrives. what opens the door?
games.why: Maitreya snaps his fingers, the door opens, and the tower inside turns out to be as wide as the sky.

practice: Rest one hand in your lap and look at it. Let it open the way the tower did: every hand it has held, every meal it has lifted, every door it has opened, years of days inside it without the hand growing any bigger.
Then come back to just the hand, resting there, its own size.

wordCard.voice: Maitreya's tower. The tower Sudhana enters at a snap of the fingers, where every tower holds all the others. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a many-storied pavilion or tower, the kind of building Maitreya's tower is called.

carryVoice: Your line: every room holds all. A snap of the fingers, and the road turned inside out. I'll be here tomorrow.
